newsitem.title: USA: Holiday shopping season off to good start-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Holiday shopping season off to good start-analysts.

text.p: Americans were in a buying mood at the beginning of the holiday shopping season, flocking to shopping centers and malls to quench a pent-up desire to buy gifts for loved ones, analysts and retailers said Sunday.

The apparent buying frenzy has been sparked by increased consumer confidence about the economy and five fewer shopping days between Thanksgiving and Christmas -- meaning shoppers were more willing to spend more money and spend it more quickly.
"There's a sense of prosperity around, and I think people are spending a buck or two for gifts," said Howard Eilenberg, analyst at Johnson Redbook, a unit of Lynch, Jones & Ryan, Inc.

Shopping at malls was up 11 percent on Friday, traditionally the busiest shopping day of the year, over the prior year, according to a national sample of regional malls compiled by the International Council of Shopping Centers.
The trade group said that was the largest increase for that day since it began tracking sales in 1993.
The numbers were fueled by a 14.2 percent jump in footwear, a 16.6 percent increase in jewelry, and a 14.3 percent increase in food sales.
In addition, apparel sales were up six percent over last year, music and entertainment and software were up 8.9 percent, and cards and gifts and books were up 11.5 percent.
The figures were based on sales at 24 malls representing about 1,000 specialty stores. They do not include department stores and other mall anchor stores.

"Usually, the day after Thanksgiving is mostly a day for browsing, but I saw more shopping bags Friday than in any other year we've been tracking this," said John Konarski, vice president of the trade group's research.
He said the heavy shopping is partly the result of a better economy and the fewer shopping days between Thanksgiving and Christmas, prompting shoppers to get an early jump on gift buying.
TeleCheck Services, a subsidiary of First Data Corp, which measures shopping done by checks it has authorized, said same-store retail sales on Friday were up 3.6 percent over the prior year.
TeleCheck Senior Economist William Ford said that based on the first shopping day, "TeleCheck anticipates a two- to four-percent same-store sales gain during the entire holiday shopping period."
Shoppers wrote 2.7 percent more checks than in the prior year's day-after-Thanksgiving, and the average amount of checks rose to $90.56 compared with $89.72, he said.

"Consumers are more confident this year, incomes are up and more people have jobs, which should result in an improved retail picture this holiday season," Ford said. "Cool weather across much of the country seems to have gotten people into the holiday spirit, and many shoppers may have realized they have five fewer days to complete their shopping."

At the Mall of America in Bloomington, Minn., spokeswoman Teresa McFarland said the mall had its "best-ever weekend after Thanksgiving," with some stores reporting sales increases of 35 percent over the previous year.
"We saw a lot of shoppers carrying a lot of bags out of the mall at 10 o'clock," she said.

Retailers and analysts said some of the more popular items this seasons are Nintendo Co Ltd's Nintendo 64, Tyco Toys In'cs "Tickle Me Elmo" toy, fleece apparel, and household items, such as breadmakers.

Susan Eich, a spokeswoman for Dayton Hudson Corp, said sales at the company's 64 department stores are slower this year than last but are "on plan." Its Target chain of stores was seeing its strongest sales in electronics, propelled largely by Nintendo 64, which sells for about $199.
Its Mervyn's chain was coming in "slightly better than expectations" so far, with strong showings in the "basics," she said, of infant and toddler clothing, intimate apparel and jewelery.
The five fewer holiday shopping days was expected to be a drag on overall results, Eich said.
"Any time you remove five days between those windows, you're going to affect your sales volume," she said, adding that the company has sought to be conservative in its inventory levels to compensate.
At Sears, Roebuck and Co, Senior Executive Vice President John Costello said the department store is "encouraged" by what it has seen so far.
Costello said sales appear to be up across the board -- from men's and children's apparel to its brand of Craftsman tools and fine jewelery.
"Consumer optimism is up and it looks like consumers are responding to the short season by getting an earlier start," Costello said.
Analysts and retailers were quick to caution that Friday's results are a mere snapshot in time and cannot serve as the sole barometer for the entire shopping season.
However, many were confident that this year's season would post a stronger showing than in 1995, when consumers held on tight to their wallets.
"It should be a good season," Johnson Redbook's Eilenberg said. "It certainly will be better than a year ago. There's no question about that."
